analysis|02-05|1597|Εκτελούνται οι Ιάπωνες χριστιανοί του Ναγκασάκι|Japanese Christians are executed at Nagasaki|At the end of the 16th century Christianity had reached Japan through European missionaries, mainly Jesuits, and had gained a number of followers in the urban areas and at court. The authority that unified the country was worried about foreign influences and about the possible alliance of the missionaries with foreign powers. Toyotomi Hideyoshi regarded the Christians as a threat to the political order and to central administration. He had already issued edicts against the missionaries. // On 5 February 1597, at Nagasaki, twenty-six Christians were crucified, among them missionaries, Japanese clergy and ordinary believers. The execution was carried out publicly, so that it would serve as a warning to those who followed the new religion, after a march of many days to the city. The martyrs faced death with courage, and their story spread quickly. // The execution of the martyrs became a symbol of the persecution of Christians in Japan, which continued for decades. The Catholic Church later recognised them as saints. Their story remains part of the memory of the Japanese Christian community and of the country's relationship with the West. The accounts of the martyrs are read today also as testimony on religious freedom.

analysis|02-05|1852|Ανοίγει το Ερμιτάζ|The Hermitage opens to the public|Saint Petersburg was the capital of the Russian Empire and the centre of the imperial court. For decades the tsars had gathered large collections of works of art, which were kept in the palaces for reasons of prestige and personal enjoyment. The collection had been greatly enriched in the time of Catherine the Great, with objects that were bought or acquired from Western collections. // In February 1852 the Hermitage opened to the public for the first time, at a time when museums in Europe were becoming ever more accessible. The site, which until then had functioned as a private collection of the court, began to operate as a public museum with specific rules and opening hours. This transition required organisation, safekeeping and careful conservation of the works. // The conversion of the Hermitage into a public museum is regarded as an important step for the culture of Russia. The museum developed gradually, adding new wings and new collections, and today it is one of the largest and best-known museums in the world. Public access to the works of art became part of the education and national identity of the country. Today the Hermitage hosts millions of visitors every year and is linked with the name of Saint Petersburg, one of the most important cultural centres of Europe.

analysis|02-05|1971|Το Απόλλων 14 προσεληνώνεται|Apollo 14 lands on the Moon|After the landing of Apollo 11 in 1969, NASA continued its missions to the Moon with the aim of exploring areas with different geology. The Apollo 13 mission had been prevented from landing after a failure, and the next flight had to demonstrate that the system could work again safely. The astronauts had been intensively trained in geological observation and in sample collection. // On 5 February 1971 the craft landed in the Fra Mauro region, where Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell carried out walks on the surface. Shepard became the fifth man to set foot on the Moon, while the instruments and samples were carried with a hand-operated transport vehicle. The two astronauts collected rocks and soil material for laboratory analysis. // The mission was the third crewed lunar landing and contributed to a better understanding of the geological history of the Moon. The samples helped scientists to estimate the age and composition of the rocks. The mission, together with the others, showed that crewed flights could carry out complex scientific activities beyond a short stay. Scientific instruments left by the mission on the Moon continued to record data for some years after the astronauts' departure.

analysis|02-06|1819|Ο Ράφλς ιδρύει τη Σιγκαπούρη|Raffles founds Singapore|At the beginning of the 19th century the British East India Company was looking for a station in the straits that connect the Indian and Pacific Oceans, in order to protect its trade. The area was controlled by Dutch forces and local rulers, while the position of the island was strategically very important. Stamford Raffles, a British official with wide experience in the region, undertook to secure a British presence. // On 6 February 1819 Raffles signed an agreement with the local ruler that allowed the founding of a trading post on the island. The settlement began quickly, with a port, warehouses and free trade, which attracted merchants from many areas of Asia. The rapid development made the new centre attractive for shipowners and migrants. // Singapore developed into a major commercial and maritime centre, at one of the busiest sea passages in the world. The founding changed the balance with the Dutch forces in the region and laid the foundations for the future British presence. Today Singapore is an independent state of great economic importance. The city quickly became a hub for trade, shipping and transport, and its history is bound up with the shaping of the modern Asian economy.

analysis|02-06|1840|Η Συνθήκη του Ουαϊτάνγκι|The Treaty of Waitangi|Before 1840 New Zealand was an island territory with a growing British presence, mainly of traders, missionaries and settlers. The Māori were the indigenous community, with their own social organisation and land rights. Tensions grew as the purchase of land by Europeans created doubts about the future of the chiefs, and the British government wished to regulate the relationship. // On 6 February 1840, at Waitangi, the British government and several Māori leaders signed the text of the treaty. The text provided for the recognition of British sovereignty but also for the retention of the lands and rights of the Māori. The treaty was written in English and in Māori, and the two versions did not always coincide in their wording. // The treaty is regarded as the founding document of New Zealand, but its implementation caused a long dispute over Māori rights. In the 20th century it was recognised as a basis for reconciliation and for processes of redress, and today it is a central point of national debate. Its significance is twofold, as a legal text and as a symbol of the relationship between the peoples of the country. The difference between the texts remains a subject of study to this day, particularly for the translation of the terms concerning sovereignty and land.

analysis|02-06|1918|Οι γυναίκες πάνω από 30 ετών ψηφίζουν|Women over 30 gain the vote|At the end of the First World War Britain faced strong pressure to widen the electorate. The suffragette movement had fought for decades, and the participation of women at the front and in the factories strengthened the argument for political equality. The government also wished to broaden the basis of the vote after great changes in society. // The Representation of the People Act, passed in February 1918, gave the vote to women over 30 who met certain property qualifications or were connected with a university. This arrangement increased the electorate to about eight million women. At the same time the law extended the right to vote to most men. // The reform was not complete, since women under 30 did not yet have equal treatment. Full equality came in 1928, when the vote was given to all women on the same terms as men. The decision of 1918 is regarded as an important step towards the democratic widening of British society, and it marked the gradual removal of obstacles to political participation. The reform was linked with a broader change in social attitudes to the role of women in public life and at work.

analysis|02-06|1922|Η ναυτική συνθήκη της Ουάσινγκτον|The Washington Naval Treaty|After the First World War the great naval powers were competing in an international arms race, with battleships and heavy cruisers as the main weapons. The cost was enormous, and Japan, the United States and Britain were worried about the intentions of the others. The competition in the Pacific made the need for an agreement even more urgent. // The United States, Britain, Japan, France and Italy gathered in Washington, and on 6 February 1922 the treaty was signed. The agreement set quotas for the number and size of large warships, based on a specific ratio among the powers. The conference also dealt with questions of security in the Pacific and in China. // The treaty is regarded as an important attempt to avoid a new naval race after the war, and for a time it noticeably limited expenditure. However, the quotas did not satisfy everyone, and Japan felt wronged, which later contributed to the tensions before the Second World War. The agreement remains an example of the international diplomacy of the interwar period. The treaty was one of the first attempts at international limitation of armaments in history, and it remained a point of reference for later negotiations.

analysis|02-06|1952|Η Ελισάβετ Β΄ γίνεται βασίλισσα|Elizabeth II becomes queen|In 1952 the British monarchy faced the postwar challenges of economic recovery and decolonisation. King George VI had come to the throne after his brother's abdication, and his health had long been fragile. His daughter Elizabeth was the heir and at that time was on an official journey in Kenya. // On 6 February 1952 the king died at Sandringham, and Elizabeth, then 25 years old, immediately succeeded to the throne of the United Kingdom. The transition took place in accordance with the customary and constitutional framework, without particular disturbance to the political system. The new queen announced that she would keep her name, and her coronation took place later, in 1953. // Her reign, which lasted for more than seven decades, was linked with deep changes in Britain and in the Commonwealth. The monarchy adapted to modern society, keeping a mainly ceremonial and symbolic role. The beginning of her reign is regarded as a turning point in the development of British public life. Her reign was linked with the reorganisation of the Commonwealth, in which many countries gained independence while remaining members of the family of nations. The transition to the new queen was accompanied by wider discussions about the role of the monarchy in modern democracy.

analysis|02-06|1958|Η καταστροφή του Μονάχου|The Munich air disaster|In the mid-1950s Manchester United was among the leading clubs in England and had stood out for its young players, who moved its supporters. The club took part in the European Cup, and air travel for teams was still rare and often dangerous. International matches often required long journeys with limited facilities. // On 6 February 1958, on the return from a match in Belgrade, the aircraft made an intermediate stop at Munich to refuel. During take-off from the stop at Munich the aircraft crashed, and 23 people were killed, among them several players of the team and journalists. The tragedy shocked the country and the world of sport. // The disaster remains in history as one of the best-known air accidents in football, and the club was gradually rebuilt around the survivors. Its story became a symbol of memory and resilience for supporters, with many events each year honouring the victims. It also led to discussions about the safety of transport. The lives of the victims remain in the memory of the club, which honours them with regular events and memorial services. The incident has also been discussed as an example of the need for better safety in flight.

analysis|02-06|1959|Επιτυχής δοκιμή του πυραύλου Τιτάν|Successful test of the Titan missile|At the end of the 1950s the United States and the Soviet Union were competing to develop long-range missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads. The American side wished to acquire a reliable system for missile defence and strategic deterrence, and for that reason it carried out continuous tests. The era was marked by an intensely competitive atmosphere and by the space race that was beginning. // In February 1959 the Titan missile was launched from Cape Canaveral, in a test that was regarded as successful. The missile was designed for long range and was based on two stages, a feature that made it an important step for American intercontinental systems. The test confirmed the operation of the propulsion and guidance systems. // The Titan formed part of the American strategic force for several years, and its programmes contributed to the development of later missiles and space launchers. Its success showed that industry could build reliable large-scale systems. The test is thus linked with the wider history of the Cold War and of the space race. The success of the test was important for the programme, because it showed that the technology was ready for further development and for more complex missions.

analysis|02-07|1497|Η «Πυρά της Ματαιοδοξίας» στη Φλωρεντία|The "Bonfire of the Vanities" in Florence|At the end of the 15th century Florence was in political turmoil after the expulsion of the Medici in 1494. The city's main political and religious leader was Girolamo Savonarola, a preacher who denounced luxury, the corruption of the clergy and the vanity of the rich. His influence was great, particularly among the young and the poorer citizens. // On Shrove Tuesday, 7 February 1497, followers of Savonarola gathered in the city square books, paintings, mirrors, cosmetics and other objects that they regarded as harmful or immoral. These objects were burned in public in a ceremony that became known as the "Bonfire of the Vanities". The act provoked strong reactions in the circles of artists and merchants. // The event shows the depth of the religious and political tension of the era. Savonarola was eventually condemned and executed in 1498, and the story of the bonfires is today used as an example of the conflict between freedom of expression and fanaticism. The episode is often discussed in accounts of the Italian Renaissance, as an example of the tension between art and the moral criticism of the era. The account of the execution continues to be debated in historiography, with emphasis on the contradictions of the period.

analysis|02-07|1795|Η 11η τροπολογία του αμερικανικού Συντάγματος|The 11th Amendment to the American Constitution|At the end of the 18th century the young American federation faced many questions about the relationship between central authority and the states. Following a court case involving Georgia and citizens of another state, the Supreme Court recognised the possibility of suing states in federal courts. This decision provoked strong reaction, because it appeared to threaten the sovereignty of the states. // The 11th Amendment was ratified on 7 February 1795 and restricted the ability of citizens of one state to sue another state in federal courts. In this way the balance between the federation and the states was restored, in line with the views of the founders. The amendment was passed quickly, in order to correct the disputed interpretation. // The amendment forms part of the system of changes that keep the Constitution flexible in the face of developments. Its interpretation remained a subject of debate for centuries, particularly in cases concerning the limits of federal jurisdiction. Today it is regarded as a basic element of the American constitutional balance between the federation and the states. The debate over the limits of federal jurisdiction continues to this day, and the history of the amendment shows how often the Constitution of the United States is reinterpreted.

analysis|02-07|1964|Οι Beatles φτάνουν στις ΗΠΑ|The Beatles arrive in the United States|In the early 1960s the British rock scene was still developing, while other genres and artists dominated in the United States. The Beatles had already become a great success in Britain and in Europe, and their record company was trying to secure the release of their records in the American market. The promotional campaign had begun to create expectations. // On 7 February 1964 the group arrived at New York's airport, where they were welcomed by thousands of young fans, many of whom had gathered for hours. The scene created a great sensation in the press and in music circles. Shortly afterwards the musicians appeared on television and at their first concerts in the United States. // The arrival is regarded as the beginning of the "British Invasion", a wave of British groups that came to dominate American charts and performances. This influence changed the trends of pop music and inspired many future generations of musicians. The event is regarded as a turning point in the relationship between young people and the music industry. This influence was broad and concerned fashion, the language of young people and the way young people viewed their society.

analysis|02-07|1974|Η Γρενάδα γίνεται ανεξάρτητη|Grenada becomes independent|Grenada is a Caribbean island that for centuries was under British rule, with an economy based mainly on agriculture, and especially on spices. In the 20th century the road towards self-government opened gradually, under conditions that characterised many colonies of the region. Autonomy became progressively wider, and the island acquired its own parliament and political institutions. // On 7 February 1974 Grenada became an independent state and continued to take part in the Commonwealth of Nations, with the British monarch as head of state. The transition took place smoothly, with the local authorities fully taking over the responsibilities of government. Independence was regarded as a milestone for the island's national self-confidence. // Independence opened the way to the development of the state, but the island's political life later experienced intense tensions and changes of government. In 1983 the territory was at the centre of international developments, when foreign forces intervened on the island. The history of Grenada shows the difficulties faced by the small states of the region in securing stability and economic independence. Independence was completed while keeping certain ties with the United Kingdom, such as the shared monarch, which remains to this day.

analysis|02-07|1990|Το Κομμουνιστικό Κόμμα εγκαταλείπει το μονοπώλιο της εξουσίας|The Communist Party gives up its monopoly on power|At the end of the 1980s the Soviet Union was in a deep economic and political crisis, with Gorbachev's reform policy causing strong conflicts. Political freedoms had been widened, while public debate was becoming more open. The Communist Party, which for decades had been the only legal party, faced growing challenge. // In early February 1990 the Central Committee of the party accepted that its role as the only party in power should end, which was a radical change. The decision opened the way for other parties and for free political debate. The announcement was made during a plenary session of the party and was regarded as a historic event. // The decision led gradually to a multi-party system and to free elections, which changed the constitutional and institutional structure of the country. The USSR was dissolved shortly afterwards, in 1991, while the changes also affected the course of the countries of Eastern Europe. This decision is regarded as one of the critical steps at the end of the Cold War and of the Soviet era. The continuation of the process showed that the changes were profound, since the political power of the party began to weaken and the institutions were reshaped.

analysis|02-07|1992|Υπογράφεται η Συνθήκη του Μάαστριχτ|The Maastricht Treaty is signed|After the fall of the Berlin Wall and the reunification of Germany, the European countries sought a new form of cooperation that would strengthen economic and political unity. The idea of a monetary union had already been discussed for years, and the need for a common political approach to questions of security and migration was becoming pressing. The negotiations were complex and often difficult. // On 7 February 1992 the twelve countries of the then European Community signed the treaty at Maastricht in the Netherlands. The treaty established the European Union and provided for a single currency, as well as a common foreign policy and cooperation in home affairs. The signing was important because the field of European cooperation was widened. // The treaty prepared the way for the euro, which was later introduced as the common currency of many countries on the continent. Its success brought new challenges, such as the differences between the economies of the members and democratic reactions to decisions taken in Brussels. Today Maastricht is regarded as the founding text of the modern European Union. The establishment of the European Union also provided a new framework for cooperation on justice matters and for the free movement of people and goods.

analysis|02-08|1587|Εκτελείται η Μαρία Στιούαρτ|Mary, Queen of Scots, is executed|Mary Stuart was queen of Scotland, who had been forced to abdicate and had taken refuge in England in 1568. Her presence at the court of Elizabeth I caused constant tension, because she had Catholic claims to the English throne and was a point of reference for Catholic plots. For almost twenty years she was kept under strict surveillance. // Her arrest followed the discovery of a plot to assassinate Elizabeth, as did the trial that followed, on a charge of conspiracy. The execution took place on 8 February 1587 at Fotheringhay Castle, by beheading. The decision was examined with great care by the English justice system, but its political significance was decisive. // The execution intensified the opposition between the English Protestant state and the Catholics of Europe, and it provided an occasion for the tensions that later led to the Armada of 1588. Mary's figure remains in history as a symbol of the political tragedy of the monarchies of the era. Her death permanently changed the international balance of power in Britain. The story of the execution was later linked with subsequent narratives and plays, which made Mary a symbol of the tragic fate of royal figures. The history of the execution is still debated, since the sources of the era do not always agree on the earlier steps of the affair.

analysis|02-08|1904|Η ιαπωνική επίθεση στο Πορτ Άρθουρ|The Japanese attack on Port Arthur|At the end of the 19th century Russia and Japan were competing for influence in Manchuria and Korea. Russia had acquired the Port Arthur area, a strategic port in China, and the Japanese government considered that the Russian presence threatened its interests. Diplomatic negotiations were deadlocked, and war now seemed unavoidable. // On 8 February 1904 Japanese ships attacked the Russian fleet that lay at anchor outside Port Arthur, without warning before the naval attack. The blows caused serious damage to Russian ships and opened the war. The attack developed into one of the most intense clashes of the era in the East. // The Russo-Japanese War began with this attack and lasted until 1905, with major battles on land and at sea. Japan won the war, and its victory revealed a new great power in Asia. The clash is regarded as a turning point in the balance of power in the region and was a warning for the decades that followed. The defeat of the Russian fleet was one of the significant blows to Russian strategic strength in the East, with international consequences.

analysis|02-08|1924|Η πρώτη εκτέλεση με αέριο|The first execution by gas|At the beginning of the 20th century many American states were seeking new ways of carrying out death sentences that were regarded as more humane than the earlier hanging. The electric chair had been introduced earlier, but electrocution had been criticised for the pain and technical problems it caused. The debate over methods was intense among public opinion and in legal circles. // On 8 February 1924 the state of Nevada used a gas chamber for the first time to execute a condemned man. The method was based on gas released in an enclosed space, and the procedure was recorded as a new technology of killing. The event provoked discussion about the ethical and technical aspects of the method. // The use of the gas chamber spread to other states, but the method was later largely abandoned because of the reactions and international criticism. This practice is linked with the wider debate about the humane treatment of prisoners. The event remains part of the history of the death penalty in the United States. This method, which was used for a short time in the United States, was much debated and is now cited as an example of the effects of technology on the application of punishments.

analysis|02-08|1950|Ιδρύεται η Στάζι|The Stasi is established|After the Second World War Germany was divided into occupation zones, and in the eastern zone a state under Soviet influence was founded. The new government of East Germany sought to control society and to neutralise opposition, while the security services were already in operation. The need for a powerful surveillance apparatus became more intense after the uprisings and reactions of the era. // On 8 February 1950 the Ministry for State Security, known as the Stasi, was officially established, and it organised an extensive network of informants. The service monitored citizens, parties, churches and artists, and collected files containing personal information. Its size was enormous in relation to the country's population. // The Stasi became a symbol of the East German regime and of the suppression of freedom, with consequences for the lives of millions of people. After the fall of the Wall in 1989 its archives were opened to citizens, so that they could study the case of their surveillance. Its history remains today a basic part of the debate about memory and democracy. The history of the Stasi is linked with the study of fear and control in totalitarian regimes, and it serves as teaching material for modern societies.

analysis|02-08|1963|Ανατρέπεται ο Κασέμ στο Ιράκ|Qasim is overthrown in Iraq|In the early 1960s Iraq was in political instability, with Prime Minister Abd al-Karim Qasim having come to power after the overthrow of the monarchy in 1958. Conflicts between different political groups were constant, and the Ba'ath Party had growing influence in the army and in society. The internal rivalry became particularly intense in early 1963. // On 8 February 1963 a coup was carried out by officers and politicians of the Ba'ath Party, which overthrew Qasim. The prime minister was executed shortly after his overthrow, and power passed to the coup leaders. The situation was fluid, with changes of government and clashes over the following months. // The overthrow opened a period of tension in Iraqi politics, and the Ba'ath Party was later consolidated in power. These events affected the stability of the region and Iraq's relations with its neighbours. The period is regarded as pivotal in the country's modern history. The overthrow of Qasim followed the course of Iraqi political parties, which would shape the country and the region in the years to come. The new leadership gradually strengthened its control of power, and internal instability continued for several years.

analysis|02-09|1861|Ο Τζέφερσον Ντέιβις εκλέγεται πρόεδρος των Συνομοσπονδιακών|Jefferson Davis is elected president of the Confederates|In the mid-19th century the differences between the North and South of the United States over slavery and states' rights had reached an acute crisis. After Lincoln's election in 1860, seven southern states seceded from the Union and formed the Confederacy. The new union needed common leadership and a single government structure to face the crisis. // On 9 February 1861, in Montgomery, Alabama, delegates of the seceded states chose Jefferson Davis as president. Davis was a former United States secretary of war and senator, with experience in politics and in the army. His selection strengthened the image of a serious and organised government. // Davis's election laid the foundations for the Civil War, which broke out a few weeks later. The Confederacy was governed by Davis's administration until its collapse in 1865, with historic consequences for slavery and for the unity of the country. This election remains one of the critical events of American history. The defence of slavery was a central element of the seceding states, and Davis's election became the starting point for organising the government that would face the civil war.

analysis|02-09|1870|Ιδρύεται η Εθνική Μετεωρολογική Υπηρεσία των ΗΠΑ|The United States National Weather Service is established|Before 1870 weather forecasts in the United States were unsystematic and were based on private observations, while the economy and shipping needed reliable information. The idea of a state weather service had been discussed in Congress for years. Scientists proposed systematic recording and analysis of meteorological data. // On 9 February 1870 President Grant signed the resolution of Congress that established the first state weather service. The service undertook to collect observations, issue forecasts and warn of dangers such as storms. The task was assigned to a military signal corps, which already had experience in telegraphic communications. // The creation of the service laid the foundations for meteorology as a public function in the United States. Over time the service was transferred to a civilian body and developed into the present National Weather Service, which provides forecasts for every state. The reliability of forecasts has contributed to the safety of citizens and of shipping. The history of the service shows the importance of scientific observation for public policy. The service's importance for preventing storms and for the safety of sailors and farmers was very great, particularly in times of extreme weather.

analysis|02-09|1893|Πρεμιέρα του «Φάλσταφ»|Premiere of "Falstaff"|At the end of the 19th century Italian opera was in a period of great change, with Verdi already well known for works such as Aida and Rigoletto. The composer, who had withdrawn for several years, returned to the stage with a comic work, in contrast to the dramatic works of the previous period. The choice was bold and created great expectation in the musical world. // On 9 February 1893 the opera "Falstaff" was first performed at La Scala in Milan. The work was based on Shakespeare and on the stories of the comic hero Falstaff, with lively music and clever orchestration. The premiere was received with appreciation by the audience and by the critics. // The opera is regarded as one of Verdi's last and most mature works, and it is often cited as proof of his creativity in old age. Its orchestral writing and the lightness of its style have influenced many later composers. Today "Falstaff" belongs to the core repertoire of the great operas and is often staged in international theatres. The opera remains a living work, with music that combines satire and the vitality of the orchestra, and it is often presented as an example of the composer's maturity.

analysis|02-09|1895|Εφευρίσκεται το βόλεϊ|Volleyball is invented|At the end of the 19th century American physical educators were looking for games for workers and for young men's association members that would be less rough than basketball and could be played indoors. Basketball had been invented a few years earlier and had quickly attracted attention. The need for exercise, sociability and recreation was great, particularly in the urban centres. // William Morgan, a physical education teacher in Massachusetts, devised in early 1895 a gentle game with a net, which was initially named "mintonette". The rules were simple, with teams exchanging the ball over a net without contact. The game could be played by many players and did not require great physical attributes. // Volleyball spread quickly in schools, clubs and young men's associations in the United States, and later throughout the world. Today it is one of the most popular team sports, with Olympic tournaments and professional leagues. Its creation shows how a simple idea of physical exercise can develop into a global sport. The spread of volleyball was linked with the need for shared exercise in schools and military units, while its rules were later refined for international competitions.

analysis|02-09|1964|Οι Beatles στο σόου του Εντ Σάλιβαν|The Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show|In February 1964 the Beatles had already arrived in the United States, and American publicity for the group was rising rapidly. Television was the main source of news and entertainment for families, and the big shows had enormous audiences. An appearance on such a programme was regarded as decisive for the recognition of an artist. // On 9 February 1964 the Beatles appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show, before about 73 million viewers. The appearance is regarded as one of the largest television appearances of the era, with live music and the participation of the audience. The audience figure was then the largest that had been recorded for an entertainment programme. // The appearance strengthened the group's popularity in the United States and helped the dominance of British music on American charts. It marked a new era for the television broadcasting of rock music and for the relationship between the audience and the artists. The moment remains one of the best-known points in the history of pop culture. The appearance became a reference point in the history of pop, and many later artists regard it as a turning point. The experience remains in memory as an example of how television can influence the development of music.

analysis|02-09|2018|Τελετή έναρξης των Χειμερινών Ολυμπιακών Αγώνων της Πιόνγκτσανγκ|Opening ceremony of the PyeongChang Winter Olympics|The 2018 Winter Olympic Games were held in South Korea, in a period of tension between South and North Korea. The participation of North Korea was uncertain for a time, but it was eventually decided that it would take part. The event was regarded as an opportunity for dialogue, despite the tense political atmosphere of the region. // The opening ceremony took place on 9 February 2018 in PyeongChang, where athletes from the two Koreas marched together under a common flag, as a symbol of unity. The parade produced strong emotion among the audience, although the question of political cooperation remained open. The moment was recorded as historic in Olympic history. // The cooperation of the two Koreas at the Games did not lead to a lasting political agreement, but it left a symbol of hope for the future of the peninsula. Olympic history is now linked with the tensions, the diplomatic efforts and the debate about peace. The ceremony remains one of the most symbolic moments of modern Olympic tradition. The event was widely reported by the media and for a time emphasised the idea of a shared presence of the two Koreas in the sporting arena. The Games and the ceremony were widely discussed and regarded as a symbolic event for the diplomacy of sport.

analysis|02-10|1763|Η Συνθήκη των Παρισίων|The Treaty of Paris|The Seven Years' War had involved almost all the great European powers, but the decisive conflicts also took place in the colonies. Britain and France were competing for control of trade and territory in North America and in India. The war had exhausted the finances of both countries. // On 10 February 1763 the Treaty of Paris was signed, ending the Seven Years' War. France ceded to Britain Canada and many territories of North America, while Spain lost Florida. The agreement recognised British naval and colonial supremacy in the world. // The treaty changed the map of America and laid the foundations for new tensions. The British taxes on the American colonies that followed, intended to cover the costs of the war, contributed to the revolution that broke out a few years later. The French defeat also left deep marks on France's internal politics. The treaty changed the geopolitical balance in North America and in India, with consequences that are debated to this day. The loss of Canada was a crippling blow to French colonial presence. analysis|02-10|1840|Η Βικτώρια παντρεύεται τον Αλβέρτο|Victoria marries Albert|Queen Victoria had come to the British throne in 1837 at the age of 18, and the need for a husband and heir was keenly felt in the political life of the country.
